content: Melasma, also referred to as chloasma or the mask of pregnancy when it occurs in pregnant women, is characterized by tan or dark discoloration of the facial skin. It predominantly affects women, with a female-to-male ratio of 9:1, and is more common in individuals with yellow to brown skin tones, particularly those classified as Fitzpatrick skin phototypes III to V. The condition typically develops in middle age and can persist for many years. However, in postmenopausal women, the lesions often fade spontaneously. Prolonged exposure to sunlight is the most significant etiological factor contributing to melasma. It is also observed in men and women of Native American descent (on the forearms) and individuals of German or Russian Jewish descent (on the face). The primary symptom of melasma is the appearance of brown to dark brown irregular patches, most commonly located on the mid-face, upper cheeks, nose, lips, upper lip, and forehead. Early lesions are characterized by well-defined irregular margins, while older lesions tend to exhibit a grayish-brown color with irregular and poorly defined borders. These patches often develop gradually over time. Clinically, melasma is categorized into two types: centro-facial and zygomatic. The condition does not cause any symptoms beyond the cosmetic discoloration. The pathogenesis of melasma is believed to involve the stimulation of melanocytes, or pigment-producing cells, by the female sex hormones estrogen and progesterone, leading to increased melanin production when the skin is exposed to sunlight. Women with light brown skin who reside in regions with intense sun exposure are particularly susceptible to developing melasma. Pathological studies have revealed that most cases of melasma are associated with an increased number of melanocytes, with an average increase of approximately 30%. Additionally, there is proliferation of small blood vessels in the dermis, as well as melanin deposition in the dermis accompanied by macrophages containing melanin (melanophages). These findings may explain the chronic nature of melasma. The proliferation and dilation of blood vessels may contribute to the chronicity by serving as a source of cytokines, prostaglandins, and leukotrienes that stimulate melanin synthesis. The incidence of melasma is also higher in patients with thyroid disease, and stress-induced overproduction of melanocyte-stimulating hormone (MSH) is thought to trigger outbreaks of the condition. Rare causes of melasma include allergic reactions to medications and cosmetics. Certain drugs, such as conjugated estrogens, can induce melasma. Melasma suprarenale, a symptom of Addison's disease, is particularly associated with pressure or minor skin injuries, as first described by Dr. F.J.J. Schmidt of Rotterdam in 1859. Melasma is typically diagnosed visually or with the aid of a Wood's lamp, which emits light in the 340–400 nm wavelength range. Under the Wood's lamp, excess melanin in the epidermis can be distinguished from that in the dermis. This technique allows melasma to be classified into two types: epidermal and mixed (epidermal + dermal). This differentiation is crucial for planning appropriate management strategies. The discoloration associated with melasma often resolves spontaneously over several months after childbirth or discontinuation of oral contraceptives or hormone replacement therapy. However, in cases without a clear cause, the lesions may persist for many years. For cases where the severity of the lesions warrants treatment, several therapeutic options are available: 1. Avoidance of strong sunlight exposure, particularly ultraviolet (UV) light, is essential. UVA-blocking sunscreens (320–400 nm) with a protection grade of PA+++ or higher and a sun protection factor (SPF) of 30 or more are recommended, as UVA is the most significant wavelength in stimulating hyperpigmentation. 2. Topical treatments, such as the combination of hydroquinone (2–5%), tretinoin (0.05–0.1%), and a mild corticosteroid (e.g., 0.01% dexamethasone), have been shown to be highly effective. This combination, known as Kligman's formula, has demonstrated efficacy in clearing epidermal melasma, with more than 60% of patients achieving complete clearance within three months. Currently, Tri-Luma™ (Galderma, USA) is the only FDA-approved triple-drug formulation for melasma treatment. However, potential side effects include contact dermatitis, exogenous ochronosis, confetti-like hypopigmentation, and rebound hyperpigmentation. 3. Other topical agents, such as arbutin, kojic acid, licorice extract, azelaic acid, vitamin C, soy, green tea peptides, and clove extract, have been used with varying degrees of success. While these treatments are generally less effective than Kligman's formula, they are associated with a lower incidence of complications. Many of these ingredients are found in over-the-counter skin-whitening products. 4. Chemical peels using agents like glycolic acid or alpha-hydroxy acids are popular in many countries. These peels are particularly useful for epidermal melasma but are less effective for mixed or dermal types. 5. For mixed melasma with dermal melanophages and dilated blood vessels, which are often resistant to topical treatments, more invasive methods targeting deeper layers of the skin are justified. Two laser systems have shown efficacy in treating deep melasma lesions: high-energy Q-switched Nd:YAG lasers (1064 nm) and fractional erbium glass lasers (1550 nm). The Q-switched Nd:YAG laser technique, originating in Asia, is known as laser toning and works by superficial vaporization of the epidermis, fragmentation and dispersion of melanin, and reduction of melanocytes. The fractional erbium glass laser reduces epidermal melanocytes and facilitates trans-epidermal elimination of dermal melanin. Both techniques require multiple sessions for optimal results. 6. In Asia, oral tranexamic acid (1–2 grams/day) is increasingly used for melasma treatment, although it is not FDA-approved for this indication. The most serious complication of this medication is thromboembolism, and prolonged use should be avoided. Intradermal injections of 4% tranexamic acid have also been reported as effective. After multiple laser treatments and a reduction in hyperpigmentation to near-normal skin color, maintenance therapy with effective topical agents is recommended. While a complete cure for melasma may be unlikely, lifelong sun protection and the use of topical antioxidants and safe anti-melanin synthesis agents are essential for long-term management.
